kurz: How a property is taxed on purchase, while it is held and on sale, from closing costs and property tax through rental income, depreciation and passive losses to the home sale exclusion.

bloecke.md:
For tax purposes, a property is split into two parts and taxed at three points in time. The **land** does not wear out and is never depreciated; the **building** wears out and is depreciated. On purchase, there is no federal tax, but state and local transfer taxes and other closing costs. While the property is held, local property tax is due and, if it is rented out, federal income tax on the net rental income. On sale, the gain is taxed unless the home sale exclusion applies.

Rental income is ordinary income, taxed at the regular brackets of 10% to 37%, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax above a modified AGI of $200,000 ($250,000 jointly). Losses from renting are a different matter. Rental activities are passive under 26 U.S.C. § 469, and passive losses generally cannot offset wages or portfolio income. A partial exception helps many small landlords, but it phases out with income. Together, this makes real estate tax-efficient in some respects and error-prone in many.

Every figure in a property calculation must be split between land and building. Only the building share is depreciable. A common basis for the split is the ratio in the local property tax assessment. If the purchase price is not split, either depreciation is lost or the IRS can challenge the return.

## Closing costs and transfer taxes

There is no federal tax on buying real estate. States, counties and some cities levy transfer taxes or recording taxes, and both their rates and who customarily pays them vary widely, from no transfer tax at all in some states to substantial rates in some high-cost cities. Added to this are title insurance, lender fees, appraisal, recording fees and, in some states, attorney fees. The purchase contract determines who pays what; local custom only sets the starting point for negotiation.

bloecke.md: Three rules have greater consequences than the amounts suggest. First, most closing costs on a rental are not deducted at once. They become part of the basis and, for the building share, are recovered through depreciation over 27.5 years. Second, transfers between spouses are not taxable for income tax purposes (26 U.S.C. § 1041); whether a state transfer tax applies to transfers within a family depends on state law. Third, furniture and appliances bought together with a rental can be listed separately and depreciated over five years instead of 27.5, if they are realistically valued.

## Property tax while you hold the property

Property tax is a local tax, levied by counties, cities, school districts and special districts on the assessed value of real estate. It is the main source of revenue for local governments, and the burden varies widely across the country. The calculation has three stages, which differ from place to place only in the details.

bloecke.formel: Property tax = (Assessed value − Exemptions) × Tax rate
bloecke.erklaerung: The assessor determines the value, often as a percentage of market value, state and local law set the exemptions, and the taxing districts set the rate. Rates are often stated in mills, that is dollars per $1,000 of assessed value.
variablen: value set by the county or city assessor; some states limit annual increases, California for example to 2% a year until the property changes hands
for example a homestead exemption for owner-occupied homes or relief for seniors and veterans; rental properties usually do not qualify
sum of the rates of all taxing districts, often stated in mills
bloecke.beispiel: Illustrative calculation: assessed value $300,000, homestead exemption $25,000, rate 20 mills. (300,000 − 25,000) × 0.020 = $5,500 of property tax a year.

bloecke.md:
For a rental property, property tax is an ordinary rental expense and fully deductible on Schedule E. For your own home, it is only deductible as an itemized deduction, together with state income or sales tax, under the cap on state and local taxes (SALT). Legislation in 2025 raised this cap from $10,000 to $40,000 for 2025, with small annual increases ($40,400 for 2026), reduced for incomes above $500,000 ($505,000 for 2026) but never below $10,000. Under current law, the cap returns to $10,000 in 2030. Many homeowners do not itemize at all, because the standard deduction is higher; for them, property tax has no federal tax effect.

Assessments can be appealed. If the assessed value seems too high compared with similar properties, an appeal within the local deadline can be worthwhile.

## Rental income on Schedule E

Net rental income is rents minus expenses, reported on Schedule E. Almost everything connected with the rental is deductible: mortgage interest (not principal), property tax, insurance, HOA dues, management fees, repairs, travel to the property, advertising, tax preparation for Schedule E and depreciation. The result can be negative, and in the first years of a financed rental, a loss for tax purposes is common.

The rest of the lesson works with an example property. It is a condo bought for $400,000, with $12,000 of closing costs that are added to basis, so the total basis is $412,000. Based on the county assessment, 25% is attributed to the land, so the building share is $309,000. The mortgage of $300,000 runs for 30 years at an illustrative fixed rate of 6.5%. The rent is $2,600 a month.

bloecke.titel: From rent to the tax result in the first full year
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. The tax loss of around $9,200 arises from depreciation, which is not matched by any payment. Without it, the property would show a surplus of about $2,000.

bloecke.md:
Principal is not a deductible expense. It turns cash into equity and is not a cost. A return that deducts the entire mortgage payment is wrong.

Money paid into an escrow account is not yet deductible either; property tax and insurance become deductible when the servicer pays them out. Regular HOA dues on a rental are deductible, but a special assessment for an improvement, such as a new roof for the building, has to be capitalized and depreciated.

## Depreciation and passive losses

Residential rental buildings are depreciated straight-line over 27.5 years and nonresidential buildings over 39 years, with a mid-month convention in the first and last year. Appliances, carpets and furniture in a residential rental are depreciated over five years, and land improvements such as fences or driveways over 15 years. A cost segregation study can move part of the purchase price into these shorter classes. Bonus depreciation, which the 2025 tax law restored to 100% for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, applies to these shorter-lived components, not to the building itself.

Whether the resulting loss helps you now depends on the passive activity rules. If you actively participate in managing the rental, for example by approving tenants and setting the rent, up to $25,000 of rental losses a year can offset other income. This allowance shrinks by 50 cents for each dollar of modified AGI above $100,000 and disappears at $150,000; these amounts are not indexed for inflation. Losses that are not allowed are suspended and carried forward. They are released when there is passive income or when the property is sold in a fully taxable sale. Real estate professionals who spend more than 750 hours a year and more than half of their working time in real property businesses, and who materially participate in the rental, are not subject to this limit.

bloecke.titel: Deductible rental loss by modified AGI
bloecke.unter: Special allowance for actively managed rentals under § 469(i), applied to the example loss of $9,237. From $150,000 upward, the entire loss is carried forward instead.

bloecke.md: On a sale, depreciation is recaptured. The basis is reduced by the depreciation allowed or allowable, even if you never claimed it. The part of the gain that corresponds to depreciation of the building is **unrecaptured section 1250 gain** and is taxed at your ordinary rate, but at most 25%. Only the rest of the gain gets the regular long-term rates. Depreciation therefore usually works as a deferral: it saves tax at the ordinary rate while you own the property and is taxed back at up to 25% when you sell. It becomes a permanent saving only if the property is held until death, because the heirs then receive a stepped-up basis.

## Repairs or improvements

This distinction determines whether an invoice is deducted immediately or spread over 27.5 years. **Repairs** keep the property in its ordinary operating condition, such as fixing a leak, repainting or patching a roof. They are deductible in the year paid. **Improvements** are betterments, restorations or adaptations to a new use, such as replacing all windows, a new water heater, a remodeled kitchen or an addition. They are capitalized and depreciated, for residential rental property over 27.5 years.

The tangible property regulations offer safe harbors. Items costing up to $2,500 per invoice or item can be deducted under the de minimis safe harbor. Small landlords whose building has an unadjusted basis of $1 million or less may deduct all repairs, maintenance and improvements on the building in a year if their total does not exceed the lesser of $10,000 or 2% of the building's unadjusted basis. Both require an election attached to a timely filed return.

The building's unadjusted basis is $309,000. The limit of the safe harbor for small taxpayers is the lesser of $10,000 and 2% of $309,000, that is $6,180 for the year.

- Variant A covers repainting for $1,500, a roof repair for $2,500 and a new water heater for $1,800, $5,800 in total, and stays below the limit. With the election, the entire amount is deductible immediately. At 22%, the tax effect in the first year is $1,276, provided the rental loss is deductible.
- Variant B additionally replaces the windows for $3,200, $9,000 in total, and exceeds the limit. The safe harbor is then not available for any of it. The repainting and the roof repair, $4,000, remain deductible as repairs, a tax effect of $880. The water heater and the windows, $5,000, are improvements and are depreciated over 27.5 years, that is about $182 a year, a tax effect of about $40 a year.

The windows therefore not only go into depreciation themselves but also pull the water heater with them. The limit counts all repairs, maintenance and improvements on the building in the year. Spreading larger work over two calendar years can keep each year below it.

## Selling a home or a rental

For your main home, 26 U.S.C. § 121 excludes up to $250,000 of gain from tax, or $500,000 for married couples filing jointly, if you owned the home and lived in it as your main home for at least two of the five years before the sale. The two years do not have to be continuous, and the exclusion can be used once every two years. These amounts are not indexed for inflation. For a rental, there is no exclusion. The gain is taxed in the year of sale, with depreciation recaptured as described above. A like-kind exchange under 26 U.S.C. § 1031 defers the gain if the proceeds go into another investment or business property through a qualified intermediary, with the replacement identified within 45 days and acquired within 180 days.

schritte.text: Main home, rental or both at different times? The answer decides between the § 121 exclusion, a fully taxable sale and a § 1031 exchange.
Count the months in which you owned the home and lived in it in the five years before the sale. Both tests must be met, but not necessarily at the same time.

The gain is the amount realized minus the adjusted basis. The amount realized is the sale price minus selling costs such as commissions; the adjusted basis is the purchase price plus closing costs and improvements, minus all depreciation allowed or allowable.
Depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997 for a rental or home office cannot be excluded under § 121 and is taxed as unrecaptured section 1250 gain at up to 25%.

For US sellers, usually no federal tax is withheld at closing. The closing agent reports the sale on Form 1099-S, and the tax is due with the return or through an estimated payment for the quarter of the sale.

bloecke.titel: Sale of the rental after seven years
bloecke.md:
The condo is bought in 2019 with a basis of $412,000 and rented out from then on. Depreciation of $11,236 a year gives $78,652 over seven years, simplified to full years. It is sold in 2026 for $520,000; commissions and other selling costs are $30,000.

- The adjusted basis is 412,000 − 78,652 = $333,348.
- The gain is 520,000 − 30,000 − 333,348 = $156,652.
- Of this, $78,652 is unrecaptured section 1250 gain, taxed at up to 25%, that is $19,663 for an owner in the 32% bracket. The remaining $78,000 is taxed at 15%, that is $11,700.
- The federal tax is $31,363, plus the 3.8% NIIT of about $5,953 if the owner's modified AGI exceeds the threshold, plus state tax.

Without depreciation, the gain would have been $78,000. The $78,652 of depreciation that saved tax for seven years now adds to the gain. Suspended passive losses from earlier years are released in the year of sale and reduce the tax. If the owner had kept the condo until death, the heirs would have received a basis equal to its value at that time, and neither the gain nor the depreciation would ever have been taxed.

bloecke.titel: Misconceptions about the home sale exclusion
bloecke.md:
The exclusion is often misunderstood as “lived there for two years, so the sale is tax-free”. Three limits apply. First, depreciation claimed for periods of rental or for a home office is not covered. Second, periods after 2008 in which the home was not your main home before you moved in, so-called nonqualified use, reduce the exclusion proportionally; a rental converted into a home therefore keeps part of its gain taxable. Periods of rental after you move out, within the five-year window, do not count as nonqualified use. Third, the exclusion requires that you have not used it for another home within the last two years.

A common case is renting out the former home after moving. The exclusion still applies if the sale takes place within three years after moving out, because the two-of-five-year test is then still met. After that, the full gain becomes taxable.

## Owner-occupied home

For your own home, there is no depreciation and no deduction of repairs, insurance or HOA dues. The rent you save is not taxable income. Two federal benefits remain, and both only help if you itemize. Mortgage interest is deductible on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt ($375,000 if married filing separately) for loans taken out after December 15, 2017; older loans keep the previous limit of $1 million. The 2025 tax law made these limits permanent. Property tax is deductible within the SALT cap. The federal credits for energy improvements to homes under §§ 25C and 25D ended for property placed in service or expenditures made after 2025; state and utility programs may still apply.

bloecke.titel: Renting to family below market rent
bloecke.md: If you rent a home to a relative at less than fair rental value, the days count as personal use under 26 U.S.C. § 280A. The rental is then treated like a vacation home you use yourself: expenses are only deductible up to the rental income, and no loss can arise. Renting to a relative at a fair rent as their main home, by contrast, is a normal rental. The benchmark is the rent an unrelated tenant would pay for the same home, and it has to be checked again as market rents change. A written lease, rent actually paid as agreed and no money flowing back are needed for the arrangement to stand up to scrutiny.

mitnehmen: Land is never depreciated, which is why every property calculation begins by splitting the basis into land and building.
The tax result and the cash flow systematically diverge, because depreciation reduces the result without any payment, and principal costs money without reducing the result.
Rental losses are passive; up to $25,000 a year can offset other income for actively managing landlords, but the allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified AGI.
Depreciation is recaptured on sale at up to 25%, so it mainly defers tax; it becomes a permanent saving only through the stepped-up basis at death.
For a main home, up to $250,000 or $500,000 of gain is tax-free after two of five years of ownership and use, but depreciation and nonqualified use are not covered.

The part of the gain on a sale of real property that corresponds to depreciation of the building. It is taxed at the ordinary rate, but at most 25%.

Loss from a rental or from a business without material participation, which under § 469 can generally only offset passive income. Unused losses are carried forward and released on a fully taxable sale.
Exclusion of up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for married couples filing jointly, on the sale of a main home owned and used as a main home for two of the five years before the sale.
